topic.name: Calculating the Equation of a Normal Line Using Differentiation

question.text: Find where the normal line to the curve $y = x^3$ at the point $(2,8)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
question.explanation:
Taking the derivative, we have

\begin{align*} f'(x) = \dfrac {\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} \left( x^3\right)=3x^2. \end{align*}

So the slope of the tangent line is \[ m=f'(2) = 3(2)^2 = 12, \]

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

\[ m'=-\dfrac{1}{m}=-\dfrac{1}{12}. \] Finally, the equation of the normal line is

\begin{align*} y - 8 &= -\dfrac{1}{12} ( x - (2) ) \\[3pt] y & = -\dfrac{1}{12} x + \dfrac {1}{6} +8 \\[3pt] y & = -\dfrac{1}{12} x + \dfrac {49}{6}. \\[3pt] \end{align*}

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get \begin{align*} -\dfrac{1}{12} x + \dfrac {49}{6} & =0\\ \dfrac{1}{12} x & =\dfrac {49}{6}\\ x&=98 \end{align*}

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(98,0).$

question.text: Find where the normal line to the curve $y = x^2$ at the point $(3,9)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
question.explanation:
Taking the derivative, we have

\begin{align*} f'(x) = \dfrac {\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} \left( x^2 \right)=2x. \end{align*} So the slope of the tangent line is \[ m=f'(3) = 2(3) = 6, \] and therefore the slope of the normal line is \[ m'=-\dfrac{1}{m}=-\dfrac{1}{6}. \] Finally, the equation of the normal line is

\begin{align} y - 9 &= -\dfrac{1}{6} ( x - 3 ) \\[3pt] y & = -\dfrac{1}{6} x + \dfrac {1}{2} + 9 \\[3pt] y & = -\dfrac{1}{6} x + \dfrac {19}{2}. \end{align}

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get \begin{align*} -\dfrac{1}{6} x + \dfrac {19}{2} & = 0 \\[5pt] \dfrac {19}{2} & = \dfrac{1}{6} x \\[5pt] x & = 57. \end{align*} Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(57,0).$

question.text: Find where the normal line to the curve $y = \dfrac{2}{x}+1$ at the point $(1,3)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
question.explanation:
Taking the derivative, we have \begin{align*} f'(x) & = \dfrac {\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} \left( \dfrac{2}{x} +1\right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac {\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} \left( 2x^{-1} +1\right) \\[5pt] & = -2x^{-2} \\[5pt] & = -\dfrac{2}{x^2}. \end{align*}

So the slope of the tangent line is \[ m=f'(1) = -\dfrac{2}{(1)^2} = -2, \] and therefore the slope of the normal line is \[ m'=-\dfrac{1}{m}=\dfrac{1}{2}. \]

Finally, the equation of the normal line is \begin{align*} y - 3 &= \dfrac{1}{2} (x - 1) \\[5pt] y &=\dfrac{1}{2}x -\dfrac{1}{2}+3 \\[5pt] y & =\dfrac{1}{2}x+\dfrac{5}{2}. \end{align*}

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get \begin{align*} \dfrac{1}{2}x+\dfrac{5}{2} & = 0 \\[5pt] x & = -5. \end{align*}

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $\left(\,\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-5},\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{0}\,\right).$
